title: Alternate text encodings for new UUIDs

events.summary: A user asks the draft to use the existing base32hex alphabet from RFC 4648 rather than inventing a new base32 alphabet.
A draft editor explains the custom alphabet exists so text sorts like the raw bytes, valuable for database keys, and floats switching to Crockford's base32.
The opener notes base32hex already sorts correctly but agrees Crockford's is better, as it avoids look-alike characters and accidental profanity and is used by ULID.
The editor will adopt Crockford's base32 next revision, judging a correctly sorting format a better fit than reusing the existing standard.
The opener has no objection and considers the issue resolved.
The editor closes the issue.
The opener makes a small wording change to the title.
The opener points to a separate IETF draft proposing a compact base64url or base32 UUID form.
The editor will look into it and try to collaborate with its author.
The editor reports writing to that draft's author.
The opener asks whether to reopen the issue to show work in progress.
The editor agrees and reopens.
The editor reopens the issue.
A UUID library author supports base32 or base58 to shorten UUIDs, prefers lowercase, and hopes the compact-name draft is merged in.
The editor notes the current draft has no alternate encoding but personally favours documenting Crockford's base32.
A co-editor marks the topic out of scope.
The co-editor closes the issue.
The editor links the Draft 03 pull request, which reintroduces encoding text.
The co-editor reopens the issue.
The co-editor removes the out-of-scope label.
The co-editor labels it a discussion.
The opener lists open questions: RFC 4648 bit-group encoding versus modulo arithmetic, how to write a base32 URN, letter case, and whether Crockford's lenient decoding breaks uniqueness.
The co-editor retitles the issue as a general discussion of alternate text encodings.
The co-editor reopens it and links a review thread from the Draft 03 pull request.
The library author wants lowercase whatever is chosen, lists base32 variants including Crockford, z-base-32 and geohash, mentions base58, and offers sample encodings.

The opener argues base32hex needs fewer caveats than Crockford, notes geohash is also friendly, and shows with SQL that mixed-case alphabets like base58 or base62 sort inconsistently under common collations.
The editor agrees case-sensitive formats are unwise for ordering, drafts concise Crockford encoding rules, and suggests ULID becomes compatible with UUIDv7.
The editor argues for exactly one extra format that is compact, case-insensitive, byte-order sortable and easy to tell from hex, to keep parsing simple.
The opener shows ULID's encoding differs from RFC 4648 output, so compatibility does not hold.
The editor concedes the ULID point.
The opener explains why ULID encodes its parts separately.
A contributor notes base32hex can use built-in language features, and challenges the group to compare more compact bases before settling.
The opener agrees alphabets can be translated trivially.
The contributor shows plain modulo base36 breaks sort order for extended IDs, and urges weighing bases 36, 58 and 62 rather than the easy option.
The library author restates that bases above 32 need mixed case or symbols, and now leans to unpadded geohash base32.
The contributor argues compact JSON transport may matter more than database collation, and questions the value of friendly alphabets over base32hex.
The library author shifts toward base58 or base62, arguing people copy rather than read IDs and collations can be changed.
The editor lays out the core trade-off as shorter IDs versus case-insensitive IDs versus allowing both, noting that multiple formats make parsing ambiguous.
The contributor suggests specifying both a case-insensitive and a compact format so libraries interoperate, pairing base36 with base62 or base32 with base64.
The editor reflects that an application usually picks one canonical text form and will think further.
The opener prefers base32hex, or base64url when ordering does not matter, and floats letter-only base52 and base48 alphabets.
A contributor suggests alternate encodings belong in a separate spec.
The editor insists the document must answer what a library's String method should return, or much of its value is lost.
A user asks for a source for the claim that JSON encodes binary as base64.
The contributor likes base52 for avoiding leading zeros and argues text format is urgent, though the familiar hex form should stay the default.
The library author likes both new alphabets.
A UUID library maintainer questions adding any new format, valuing one canonical form, and ties it to whether the RFC replaces or extends RFC 4122.
The editor concedes the JSON point and walks through a web-shop scenario where IDs appear in databases, email addresses, URLs and IoT payloads.
The opener says non-power-of-two bases need big-integer modulo arithmetic and shares sample code.
The contributor shares a general base conversion routine and simple base36 and base32 versions to show the code is small.
The contributor argues the text format drives people to UUID alternatives, but that the new RFC should keep 8-4-4-4-12 as the mandatory canonical form and recommend extra formats.
The opener praises the routine and suggests C code in the spec if another base is chosen.
The opener measures how often short words appear in random IDs per base, finding base36 does best.
The co-editor summarises: keep 8-4-4-4-12 as a must, allow any base, guide toward base36, and reference common methods.
The editor rejects allowing any base because parsers cannot tell formats apart, and argues for one extra hyphen-free, case-insensitive format, preferring Crockford base32 over base36.
The contributor doubts one alternative is enough given how many ID schemes use base62 or base64.
The editor says apps can still use other encodings and asks how a library's String and Parse would support two formats.
The opener sketches a default encoding plus parse and format functions that take a base or alphabet.
The library maintainer warns a format argument defeats tree-shaking in JavaScript bundles.
The contributor suspects the editor really wants Crockford as the new default and disagrees, proposing extra methods, length-based detection and showing a short C routine.
The co-editor links the Draft 03 phase 4 pull request containing the encoding section.
The editor admits they did want Crockford as the default but accepts that may be too big a change, and cites the bundle-size concern against open-ended bases.
The editor proposes keeping hex as default and adding an optional compact Crockford base32 format, while noting apps may use any encoding.
The library author would rather move to one modern format outright than keep the old one.
The contributor says changing the default would break dependants, and asks again whether base36 plus base62 is acceptable instead of an any-base approach.
The co-editor reports a first pass of the encoding section in the draft PR and fixes a sample UUID for examples.

The library maintainer finds the optional compact proposal balanced but expects to adopt cautiously, wants the any-base appendix dropped, and opposes multiple formats as against the purpose of standards.
The library maintainer compares it to imperial versus metric units and suggests a full replacement RFC may be the honest path, half in jest.
The library author argues the spec must decide between extending and modernising, and suggests either splitting the RFC or mandating one new encoding.
The contributor proposes text where 8-4-4-4-12 is mandatory and libraries should also support base36 and base62, detected by length.
The editor floats making Crockford base32 the canonical text for the new variant only, leaving older versions on hex.
A user warns Crockford's base32 is not an RFC and has loose edge cases, so may need its own spec.
The library author says implementations use Crockford's alphabet with RFC 4648's algorithm.
The contributor clarifies the recommendation targets libraries and argues standard alternatives are for interoperability, not application-specific choices.
A contributor suggests reviving the legacy UUID layout and calls other encodings the developer's choice.
The library maintainer doubts users will accept new versions without hex.
The library maintainer shows that the draft's permissive wording would allow absurd encodings such as playing cards and cuneiform.
The editor falls back to hex plus one compact format, and asks what format a database query should return if many are allowed.
A contributor argues this draft should only update RFC 4122 with new versions and says they are writing a separate draft to obsolete it.
The editor welcomes collaboration but sees the contested items as essential to make UUIDs useful.
The contributor says updating and obsoleting work should be kept apart.
The contributor clarifies they want exactly two concrete formats, one case-insensitive and one compact, and argues the second adds little cost.
The editor prefers Crockford base32 for familiarity and worries extra formats complicate parsing and invite a slippery slope.
A contributor explains the IETF difference between updating and obsoleting an RFC.
The contributor says they will follow consensus, notes base36 is built into several languages, and opposes variable-length UUIDs.
A contributor agrees new versions can update RFC 4122 but plans a separate obsoleting draft.
The co-editor summarises open engineering problems, especially how a receiver learns which encoding was used, weighing a single base, the multibase draft, or an extended URN.
A contributor prefers JSON over URNs for carrying such metadata.
The co-editor marks the topic out of scope again.
The co-editor announces that, after talking with the editor, alternate encodings are out of scope for Draft 03 and will move to a separate new draft with the E variant and long UUIDs.
The co-editor publishes Draft 00 of a separate encoding-techniques document, including an extended URN to signal encoding, and personally favours an inclusive approach.
The co-editor removes the out-of-scope label.
The library author notes a Hacker News thread where alternate encoding was the most requested feature.
The repository owner locks the issue.
The co-editor converts the issue into a discussion.
